text: You have two choices, young man. This is one. You know the other.
It was like watching a frog try to hop out of a bucket that was too high for it.
Clarissa Cottonmoon was looking at the clock. As the director of the Birchbright Theater, she was used to things running on time.
Not such cool adults now, are we?
He gave Clarissa his best puppy look, looking out from under his hair, his riverine eyes glowing with the light of a thousand second chances.
It wasn’t bleeding: it was leaking red paint.
Even though Corey was a theater kid, he had the face of a quarterback on a CW show: summer-blue eyes and artfully careless hair, jawline like a Berkshire ridge.
The stern quartz visage of the grandfather clock was poor comfort to the fidgeting miscreants, as they stood before the theater director’s desk.
It, not her, she thought sometimes, was the true theater director. There was so much to do, and her only currency for doing it was scant, unmerciful time.
Corey just looked up at her. Clarissa could swear the look on his face was vaguely smug.
Frankly, I don’t trust either of you enough right now to tell them the truth, and I can’t stand the idea of our friendships being something else you ruin by neglecting the truth.
I expect stellar behavior from now on, or you’ll be right back over my knee.
